Appendix S3 — Solver Scalability

Full script: scripts/supp_S3_scaling.R

Source: vignettes/supp-S3-scaling.qmd 
library(DeCovarT)

Script: scripts/supp_S3_scaling.R — scalability grid. Outputs in output/supp_S3/.

:one: Generative Model

Motivation

This appendix maps DeCovarT performance across the five main statistical difficulty axes identified in the full factorial plan (temp_rag_simualtions_scenarios/detailled_siulation_code.md):

Axis Range
Cell types J 2, 4, 8
Genes G 20, 50, 100, 250
Mean cosine \rho_\mu 0, 0.5, 0.9
Precision condition \kappa 3, 10, 100
Composition entropy H / \log J \approx 1.0,\, 0.75,\, 0.40

Full factorial

3 \times 4 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 324 \text{ scenarios}

N = 100 Monte Carlo replicates per scenario (smoke test: n = 2).

Realised difficulty descriptors recorded

Each generated problem stores the following descriptors for post-hoc analysis (see detailled_siulation_code.md §Difficulty descriptors):

Descriptor Formula
Normalised Shannon entropy H/\log J
Mean pairwise cosine \bar{\rho}_\mu
Contrast smallest singular value \sigma_{\min}(\boldsymbol{M})
Pairwise Bhattacharyya distance closed-form Gaussian
Covariance heterogeneity \operatorname{mean}_F distance
Precision average degree 2|E|/G
\kappa(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j) spectral condition number 
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# SECTION 1: GENERATIVE MODEL
# Build the 324-scenario grid
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
SEED <- 20260807L

scaling_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  J           = c(2L, 4L, 8L),
  G           = c(20L, 50L, 100L, 250L),
  cosine_mu   = c(0.0, 0.5, 0.9),
  kappa_target = c(3, 10, 100),
  entropy_norm = c(1.0, 0.75, 0.40)   # approx Dirichlet concentration
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    scenario_id = dplyr::row_number(),
    mu = purrr::pmap(list(J, G, cosine_mu), \(j, g, rho) {
      generate_mean_signature_matrix(
        n_cell_types      = j,
        n_genes           = g,
        cosine_similarity = rho,
        mean_scale        = 100,
        seed              = SEED + j * g
      )
    }),
    proportions = purrr::map2(J, entropy_norm, \(j, h) {
      # concentration parameter from normalised entropy
      alpha <- exp(h * log(j)) / j
      as.vector(gtools::rdirichlet(1L, rep(alpha, j)))
    }),
    covariance = purrr::pmap(list(J, G, kappa_target), \(j, g, kappa) {
      purrr::map(seq_len(j), \(jj) {
        net <- generate_random_network_skeleton(g, model = "erdos_renyi",
                                               seed = SEED + jj)
        build_normalised_precision(net, target_kappa = kappa) |> solve()
      })
    })
  )

:two: Inference 

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# SECTION 2: INFERENCE
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
N_REPLICATES <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("N_REPLICATES", unset = "100"))
ALGORITHMS   <- c("NNLS", "Marquardt-Levenberg")
dir.create("output/supp_S3", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

scaling_results <- purrr::pmap(
  dplyr::select(scaling_grid, proportions, mu, covariance),
  \(proportions, mu, covariance) {
    run_simulation_benchmark(
      n_replicates          = N_REPLICATES,
      true_proportions      = proportions,
      mean_signature_matrix = mu,
      covariance_matrices   = covariance,
      algorithm_names       = ALGORITHMS
    )
  },
  .progress = TRUE
)

saveRDS(scaling_results, "output/supp_S3/scaling_benchmark.rds")
saveRDS(scaling_grid,    "output/supp_S3/scaling_grid.rds")

:three: Visualisations

Output Description
output/supp_S3/s3_rmse_by_G.pdf RMSE vs G per cosine × kappa
output/supp_S3/s3_rmse_by_J.pdf RMSE vs J per entropy level
output/supp_S3/s3_convergence_rate.pdf Optimiser convergence rate heatmap 
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# SECTION 3: VISUALISATIONS
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
scaling_results <- readRDS("output/supp_S3/scaling_benchmark.rds")
scaling_grid    <- readRDS("output/supp_S3/scaling_grid.rds")

if (N_REPLICATES >= 10) {
  # Attach RMSE to grid
  scaling_summary <- scaling_grid |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      rmse = purrr::map_dbl(scaling_results, \(res) {
        mean(res[["Marquardt-Levenberg"]][["RMSE"]], na.rm = TRUE)
      })
    )

  p_g <- ggplot2::ggplot(
    scaling_summary,
    ggplot2::aes(G, rmse, colour = factor(cosine_mu), linetype = factor(kappa_target))
  ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line() +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~J, labeller = ggplot2::label_both) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "G (genes)", y = "Mean RMSE", colour = "Cosine μ",
                  linetype = "κ target") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()

  ggplot2::ggsave("output/supp_S3/s3_rmse_by_G.pdf", p_g, width = 9, height = 5)
}

Out-of-scope factors (full factorial plan)

The following factors from the full simulation plan are noted here but not yet implemented as they require either additional function support or substantial wall-clock time:

  • Low-rank residual r (0, 2, 8, 20): Woodbury inversion advantage.
  • Reference covariance sample size (oracle; 20; 50; 200 donors/cells): tests estimation noise rather than assuming a perfect \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. This is a critical real-data concern — estimated covariances from small single-cell cohorts add noise that is not modelled in the current simulation.
  • Connected-component structure (1, 2, 4, J-linked): predicts exact block-factorisation gains (see Appendix S2).
  • BFGS-in-ALR optimiser: a fair comparison requires implementing gradient descent in the same J-1 dimensional ALR chart as Marquardt–Levenberg; see gradient_loglik_constrained().
